You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does convincing chalk mark-making serve as the rendering medium for both the giraffes and the surrounding scene?
node.criteria: Pass if identifiable powdery or broken strokes, chalk-like contours and rubbed shading visibly render both the giraffes and their surroundings. Assess actual marks and their relationship to depicted forms, not merely an overall soft or grainy appearance. Fail if the apparent chalk medium consists only of uniform grain, blur or smearing, or if convincing chalk rendering is confined to isolated outlines while the remaining scene lacks it. Color is permitted, and neither monochrome nor a blackboard background is required. Recognizable anatomy does not itself indicate failure. Return unknown only when visual evidence is unavailable or genuinely insufficient; transport or schema failures are not negative visual evidence.
node.binding: Compare the input and edited images for the requested chalk-drawing appearance, inspecting marks and shading on the giraffes, vegetation and ground.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image has a soft, grainy appearance, but the scene is largely rendered with broad blurred or smeared areas. The giraffes retain detailed, sharp patterned contours, while the vegetation, sky, and ground lack convincing powdery or broken chalk strokes and rubbed chalk shading tied to their forms. This does not establish chalk mark-making as the medium for both the giraffes and surroundings.

The edited image has a broadly grainy, blurred and smeared appearance, but the giraffes retain mostly photographic-looking detail and sharp, dark outlines rather than convincing powdery or broken chalk strokes. The vegetation, sky and ground are largely rendered as uniform soft smears, without clear chalk mark-making tied to their forms.

The edited image has a soft, grainy appearance, but the giraffes retain mostly smooth, sharply defined photographic-like outlines and detail. The surroundings are largely blurred or smeared, with no convincing powdery or broken chalk strokes and rubbed shading visibly rendering both the animals and the scene.

The edited image has a soft, grainy, heavily smeared appearance, especially in the sky, hills, vegetation, and ground. The giraffes retain mostly smooth, sharply defined photographic-like outlines and detailed spots rather than visible powdery or broken chalk strokes and rubbed chalk shading. The surrounding scene likewise lacks convincing chalk marks tied to its forms; the overall texture is not sufficient to establish chalk rendering.

The edited image has a soft, grainy appearance, but the giraffes retain mostly smooth, sharply defined photographic-like contours and shading. The surroundings are largely blurred or smeared, with no convincing powdery or broken chalk strokes visibly rendering both the animals and the scene.

d1_drawn_representation: The binding is too vague and its “photographic forms beneath a surface effect” phrasing may bias the decision toward treating chalk texture, blur, or grain as evidence of failure. Keep the comparison anchored to the requested chalk drawing, and make the decision inspect both giraffes and the environment for actual drawn contours, marks, and shading versus retained photographic modeling; texture or smudging alone is not decisive. The traces show a real borderline distinction: the giraffes have drawn outlines and marks, while their bodies retain photographic tonal structure and much of the environment is blurred or smeared rather than clearly re-rendered. Other runs judge broad chalk-like environmental strokes sufficient. Clarify how to weigh these regions against the criterion that substantial scene areas must read as drawn, without letting one convincing region stand in for the whole scene or treating source resemblance as proof of photographic rendering. Preserve the partial-progress distinction: visible chalk-drawing changes count as progress, but do not automatically establish complete fulfillment. All traces are valid observations with no dependency or transport failures; the disagreement is semantic, not missing evidence. Repeated high-confidence variation is a calibration signal, not grounds to force a label.
